hero.headline: Port St. Lucie teen makes history as Southeast Youth of the Year, heads to national competition
hero.body:
For the first time in its history, Boys & Girls Clubs of St. Lucie County has produced a Southeast Region Youth of the Year. Enrique Rosario Liz, the valedictorian of Treasure Coast High School, earned this prestigious recognition and will now compete for the national title in New York City on October 1. The Southeast Region Youth of the Year award honors standout teenagers across the Boys & Girls Clubs community who demonstrate dedication to academics, strong personal values, and leadership through service to others.

Enrique's path to this achievement began eight years ago when he arrived in Port St. Lucie from the Dominican Republic without English language skills. With support from his school and the local Boys & Girls Club, he took advantage of every opportunity to learn and develop. "I could never have imagined this moment when I was 8 years old," Enrique said after receiving the award. "It's a privilege to share my journey, and I hope it inspires belief in every young person who needs a helping hand and an opportunity." His determination and growth have been remarkable. He has earned the titles of county Youth of the Year and Florida Youth of the Year. This fall, he will begin his studies at the University of Florida.

Will Armstead, CEO of Boys & Girls Clubs of St. Lucie County, highlighted what makes Enrique exceptional. "Enrique's achievement is historic, but his character impresses me most. He's turned challenges into opportunities and advocated for others, all with humility and determination," Armstead said. Travis Leonard, owner of A&G Concrete Pools and a longtime Youth of the Year judge, observed that Enrique distinguished himself from his peers throughout the competition process. "From the start, Enrique stood out. Thanks to his hard work and all those who support him, we finally have a Southeast Region Youth of the Year. I believe he's ready for the national competition, and I'm proud of him and our whole community," Leonard said.

Enrique's parents expressed their pride in their son's accomplishments and their gratitude for the support he has received. "We're grateful to God for every opportunity and to Boys & Girls Clubs of St. Lucie County for helping Enrique grow as a leader and a person," they said. The Youth of the Year program represents Boys & Girls Clubs of America's premier recognition for teenagers who function as role models, leaders, and change-makers within their communities.

cards.headline: Fort Pierce shooting leaves 16-year-old in critical condition, teen charged with attempted homicide
cards.teaser: A 16-year-old is facing an attempted homicide charge after a shooting Thursday night in Fort Pierce left another 16-year-old in critical condition.
cards.body:
A 16-year-old is facing an attempted homicide charge after a shooting Thursday night in Fort Pierce. According to Fort Pierce police, detectives from the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office heard gunshots while traveling on Avenue N and saw three juveniles fleeing in different directions. Another juvenile was discovered laying on the sidewalk on top of a bike with gunshot wounds.

Detectives and officers established a perimeter in the area and apprehended all three suspects. One suspect was caught by a sheriff's office K9, and another was found hiding in a recycling container. Two weapons were recovered at the scene. The 16-year-old victim remained in critical condition at a local hospital as of Friday morning. The 16-year-old suspect was arrested and charged with attempted homicide, tampering with evidence and unlawful carry of a firearm by a person under 18. He was taken to the Department of Juvenile Justice.

cards.headline: Indian River County faces $50 million budget loss from property tax amendment on November ballot
cards.teaser: Indian River County could lose around $50 million from its $597 million budget if voters approve a property tax amendment on the November ballot, according to p.
cards.body:
Indian River County leaders gathered Friday morning at the Heritage Center in Vero Beach to discuss the potential financial impact of a property tax amendment on this November's ballot. The amendment would raise the homestead exemption to $150,000 in 2027 and $250,000 in 2028. According to the Indian River County Tax Payers Association, the county's approximately $597 million budget could lose around $50 million by 2028. Vice Chair Laura Moss criticized the measure as unsound public policy, saying "They've declared war on local government." Lance Lunceford, president of the Tax Payers Association, stated there is no way to fill a hole that size without reducing law enforcement and first responder services.

Indian River Firefighters president Christen Brewer warned that fire rescue could lose $15 to $20 million of its $70 million budget, noting that 79.1% of fire rescue funding comes from ad valorem taxes. Three projected fire stations may not be built if the budget shortfall occurs. Lunceford characterized the amendment as a tax shift rather than a tax cut, potentially requiring the county to increase impact fees, utility fees, and taxes on non-homesteaded and commercial properties to compensate for lost revenue.

cards.headline: Florida economy to add 2.3 million residents by 2035 despite downgraded tourism and income forecasts
cards.body:
Florida will gain approximately 2.3 million residents between 2026 and 2035 while continuing to outpace national economic growth, according to a new economic outlook from Florida TaxWatch. The state's population is expected to grow from 23.8 million in 2026 to just over 26 million by 2035. Despite these gains, daily net migration will gradually decline from about 895 people per day to 689. Florida's appeal remains strong thanks to its business climate, absence of a personal income tax, and favorable weather, allowing the state to attract new residents even as economic headwinds persist.

The latest TaxWatch report reflects significant downgrades compared to previous forecasts. The organization cited global instability, rising energy costs, and uncertainty regarding the Strait of Hormuz as primary concerns. The statewide unemployment rate is projected to peak at 4.8% in 2027 before gradually settling near 4.2% in the early 2030s. Per-capita personal income is still expected to increase from roughly $88,000 in 2026 to more than $126,000 by 2035, but overall income projections have declined by an average of 10.3% from the prior forecast. Total employment will grow from 10.1 million workers to 11.3 million over the decade.

Tourism experienced the steepest downgrade of any sector, with visitor growth expectations falling by an average of 45.3% since the previous report. Visitor numbers are still projected to increase annually, but growth rates will slow dramatically, reaching just 0.8% growth next year. This represents the most significant impact from current economic uncertainties on Florida's major industries.

Florida's broader economy is expected to weather these challenges without major disruption. Real GDP growth will decelerate from 2.5% in 2026 to 1.9% in 2027, then rebound above 3% for much of the following decade, which actually represents an improvement compared to TaxWatch's previous forecast. According to the report, the single biggest variable shaping the outlook is uncertainty surrounding the Strait of Hormuz, through which approximately a quarter of the world's seaborne oil passes. Should energy markets stabilize, many of the more pessimistic assumptions in the forecast could improve. If not, Florida residents may face a more challenging economic path ahead.

cards.headline: Stuart attorney represents daughter of Florida Turnpike crash victim in wrongful death lawsuit
cards.body:
Angeline Dowdian, 22, has filed a wrongful death lawsuit against truck driver Harjinder Singh, White Hawk Carriers, and freight broker C.H. Robinson following the August 12, 2025 crash in St. Lucie County that killed her mother Faniola Joseph, 37, and two others. The crash occurred when Singh allegedly attempted an illegal U-turn in a clearly marked No U-turn zone on the Florida Turnpike, causing the minivan carrying Joseph, Herby Dufresne, 30, and Rodrigue Dor, 54, to become wedged underneath his semi-truck. All three people in the minivan were killed.

Angeline is represented by attorney Dax Bello of Stuart firm Tillman, Fox, Bianchi & Kane, and co-counsel Mark Brumer of Brumer & Brumer. The lawsuit alleges that C.H. Robinson, a multibillion-dollar freight broker, knowingly gave business to White Hawk Carriers despite serious safety violations in its record. Transportation expert James Lewis has publicly described White Hawk's violations as very egregious. Bello argues the crash was not an accident but a predictable end that came at the cost of three lives.

The case is bolstered by a May 14 U.S. Supreme Court ruling in Montgomery v. Caribbean Transport, which clarified that federal law does not shield freight brokers from state negligence claims when unsafe drivers are placed on the road. That ruling involved the same broker named in Angeline's case. Justice Brett Kavanaugh wrote in a concurring opinion that not all truck accidents can be prevented, but some can, noting that some carriers are known to be less safe and some truck drivers are known to be unfit.

Angeline lived in another country at the time of the crash and had not seen her mother in person in six years, though they spoke daily via video calls. On the day of the crash, she missed a call from her mother. She listens to a voice message from her mother every morning that says, Angeline, where are you? Angeline says her mother was both parents to her, since her father rejected her at birth. Singh faces criminal traffic homicide charges in Florida in addition to the civil case. White Hawk Carriers has shut down, though Bello warns they may reopen under another name.

Christen Brewer, president of Indian River Firefighters, stated that fire rescue could lose $15 to $20 million of their $70 million budget, with 79.1 percent of their funding coming from ad valorem taxes. Brewer noted that three projected fire stations may not be built if the budget shortfall occurs. Moss criticized the state's role in the amendment, calling it "an unsound, unplanned piece of public policy."

cards.headline: Delray Beach Pride memorial stalled by new state restrictions 10 years after Pulse massacre
cards.teaser: A year after the state sandblasted away Delray Beach's rainbow Pride intersection, advocates face new hurdles in creating a permanent memorial to honor the 49 victims of the Pulse nightclub shooting.
cards.body:
Friday, June 12 marks 10 years since the Pulse nightclub massacre in Orlando, where 49 people lost their lives. In Delray Beach, a rainbow-painted intersection created to honor the victims was sandblasted away by the Florida Department of Transportation in August 2025 despite city pushback. Local advocate Ronnie Dunayer and other residents formed the Delray Beach Pride Memorial Committee and designed a proposal for a rainbow pyramid monument, etched with the meaning behind each color and illuminated at night to honor the victims. They propose Old School Square, near the Eagle Scout monument and steps from where the original Pride mural stood, as the location.

The memorial faces a legal obstacle in Senate Bill 1134, which awaits the governor's decision. The bill would ban local governments from funding or supporting diversity, equity, and inclusion initiatives. It passed 25-11 in the Senate and 77-37 in the House, potentially putting state funding at risk if municipalities use city property or dollars for such projects. Commissioner Juli Casal said Delray Beach relies heavily on state funding. However, Casal noted that with private funding and private property, "it could be done tomorrow" without city involvement. Dunayer is reaching out to state leaders and national organizations to find solutions.

cards.headline: West Palm Beach motorcyclist killed in Boynton Beach crash at high speed
cards.teaser: Albert Garcia, 28, died after his motorcycle struck a car turning left at the intersection of Boynton Beach Boulevard and El Clair Ranch Road Friday morning.
cards.body:
A 28-year-old West Palm Beach man was killed Friday morning in a crash involving a motorcycle and a car at the intersection of Boynton Beach Boulevard and El Clair Ranch Road, according to the Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office. The crash happened around 7:08 a.m. Investigators said Albert Garcia was riding a 2007 Kawasaki Ninja eastbound on Boynton Beach Boulevard at a high rate of speed as he approached the intersection.

At the same time, a 2016 Kia Forte driven by a 39-year-old Boynton Beach man was stopped in the westbound lanes and attempting to make a left turn onto southbound El Clair Ranch Road. As the Kia began turning left, Garcia applied the motorcycle's brakes but did not have enough time or distance to avoid a collision. The motorcycle struck the passenger side of the Kia inside the intersection. Garcia was thrown from the motorcycle and landed a short distance southwest of the impact point. Rescue crews transported Garcia to Delray Medical Center, where he was pronounced dead. The driver of the Kia was wearing a seatbelt and was not injured. Garcia was wearing a helmet.

cards.body:
The Martin County Sheriff's Office has identified the rookie deputy involved in tackling a suspect at a golf course. The deputy was captured on video during the incident, which drew attention to the arrest.

cards.teaser: A new marina has been approved for development at a historic location in Florida, marking a significant local development decision.
cards.body:
Local officials have approved a new marina at a historic Florida site. The approval represents a major development decision for the area. Details about the specific location, size of the marina, and timeline for construction were not immediately disclosed.

The project received approval from local authorities Friday. The historic nature of the site adds significance to the development decision. Officials have moved forward with plans to bring the new marina to the area.

cards.headline: South Florida lawmakers automatically reelected without vote
cards.teaser: Several South Florida lawmakers were automatically reelected Friday without a vote, as they faced no opposition in their races.
cards.body:
Multiple South Florida lawmakers were automatically reelected Friday without a vote cast. The officials ran unopposed in their respective races, resulting in automatic reelection under Florida election law.

When candidates face no opposition by the qualifying deadline, they are declared elected without appearing on the ballot. This happened to several South Florida lawmakers Friday. The automatic reelections allow these officials to continue serving in their current positions without a contested election.

hero.headline: St. Lucie County family sues freight broker, carrier over fatal Florida Turnpike crash
hero.teaser: The daughter of a woman killed in an August 2025 crash on the Florida Turnpike in St. Lucie County has filed a wrongful death lawsuit against the truck driver, his carrier, and the freight broker.
hero.body:
On August 12, 2025, three workers traveling in St. Lucie County were killed when their minivan became wedged beneath a semi-truck. Herby Dufresne, 30, Rodrigue Dor, 54, and Faniola Joseph, 37, died in the crash after the truck driver allegedly made an illegal U-turn in a clearly marked no U-turn zone. The truck driver, Harjinder Singh, worked for White Hawk Carriers, a company with a documented history of safety violations. Joseph's daughter, Angeline Dowdian, 22, has filed a wrongful death lawsuit against Singh, White Hawk Carriers, and freight broker C.H. Robinson, claiming negligence and unsafe practices caused the tragedy.

Angeline was living in another country at the time of the crash and had not seen her mother in person for six years, though they communicated daily through video calls. She was represented by attorney Dax Bello of Stuart Tillman, Fox, Bianchi & Kane and co-counsel Mark Brumer of Brumer & Brumer. Bello argues that this crash was not an accident but a predictable outcome of negligent hiring practices. He contends that C.H. Robinson, a multibillion-dollar freight broker, knowingly continued business with White Hawk Carriers despite its serious safety violations. Transportation expert James Lewis has described White Hawk's violations as very egregious. Bello points to a May 14 Supreme Court ruling in Montgomery v. Caribbean Transport, which clarified that federal law does not protect freight brokers from state negligence claims when they place unsafe drivers on roadways. That ruling involved the same broker named in Dowdian's case.

Bello emphasized that brokers and carriers have a responsibility to verify safety records before assigning drivers to routes, noting that such information is publicly available online. He stressed that industry incentives should naturally favor safe operations. White Hawk Carriers has since shut down, though Bello warned the company may reopen under a different name, a common practice in the trucking industry. In addition to the civil case, Singh faces criminal traffic homicide charges in Florida. As a former homicide prosecutor, Bello is helping Angeline navigate both the civil and criminal proceedings under Marsy's Law, which grants victims' families rights to be informed and heard in criminal matters.

Angeline acknowledged that no legal outcome will restore what she lost. Her mother, who had hoped Angeline would become a nurse, was her primary support system after her father rejected her at birth. Visa restrictions have prevented Angeline from visiting her mother's grave. She expressed hope that the lawsuit will prevent other families from experiencing similar loss, saying she does not want others to suffer as she has. Joseph would have turned 38 on May 26, 2026.

cards.headline: Delray Beach struggles to honor Pulse victims 10 years later amid state restrictions
cards.teaser: Friday marks 10 years since the Pulse nightclub massacre in Orlando, where 49 people lost their lives. Delray Beach residents say state laws are blocking their efforts to create a memorial.
cards.body:
A Pride mural honoring Pulse nightclub massacre victims once sat at a rainbow-painted intersection blocks from downtown Delray Beach, created and funded by local residents. That memorial is now faded bricks. In August 2025, Delray Beach leaders resisted state pressure to remove the mural, arguing it occupied a city road rather than a state road. Within weeks, the Florida Department of Transportation sandblasted away the rainbow to comply with regulations on road markings and political messaging. Delray Beach initially explored legal action but abandoned the idea due to potential costs, instead proposing resources toward a new memorial.

Delray Beach residents, led by advocate Ronnie Dunayer, formed the Pride Memorial Committee and designed a proposal by March for a rainbow pyramid monument etched with color meanings and illuminated at night, to be placed at Old School Square near the Eagle Scout monument. Commissioner Juli Casal cited Senate Bill 1134, awaiting the governor's decision, as a legal barrier. The bill would ban local governments from funding diversity, equity, and inclusion initiatives. It passed 25-11 in the Senate and 77-37 in the House and could jeopardize state funding if municipalities use city property or dollars for such projects. Casal stated that private funding and private property could allow the memorial to be completed immediately.

cards.headline: Vero Beach man charged with murder of grandmother who welcomed him into her home
cards.teaser: A 29-year-old Vero Beach man is accused of killing his 76-year-old grandmother, who was found dead inside her home in February.
cards.body:
A 29-year-old Vero Beach man is accused of killing his 76-year-old grandmother, who was found dead inside her home in February. The Indian River County Sheriff's Office announced Friday that Nicholas Leonard Ivey now faces charges of murder and tampering with physical evidence in the death of Patricia Ann DiBella. Investigators said Ivey admitted to killing DiBella, his grandmother, who had opened her home to him at her residence at 5090 Fairways Circle north of Vero Beach. A welfare check requested by family members the following day led deputies to the scene, where Ivey was taken into custody. Since February, Ivey has been held on other related charges before being formally charged with murder on June 3.

Ivey is being held at the Indian River County Jail without bond. "I am proud of the work our investigations team did to bring justice to Patricia DiBella and her family. No one should lose their life at the hands of someone they trusted and welcomed into their home. I encourage anyone experiencing domestic violence to contact law enforcement," Sheriff Eric Flowers said in a statement. The sheriff's office reminded the community that domestic violence can take many forms and can affect anyone. Those in danger can call 911, SafeSpace at 772-288-7023 or the National Domestic Violence Hotline at 1-800-799-7233.

cards.headline: Nine adults and one juvenile arrested on Day 5 of St. Lucie County Operation Summer Heat
cards.teaser: St. Lucie County authorities arrested nine adults and one juvenile on the fifth day of Operation Summer Heat.
cards.body:
The St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office continued its Operation Summer Heat initiative Friday, resulting in nine adult arrests and one juvenile arrest on the operation's fifth day. The department announced the arrests as part of an ongoing effort targeting crime in the county during the summer months.

Operation Summer Heat is designed to increase law enforcement presence and proactive policing throughout St. Lucie County. The initiative focuses on addressing criminal activity across various categories during peak summer season.

hero.headline: Smithsonian Marine Ecosystems Exhibit at St. Lucie County Aquarium showcases Florida coastal habitats
hero.teaser: The Fort Pierce facility displays fully live models of ecosystems dating back to 1980 under the Smithsonian, making it unlike most public aquariums.
hero.body:
The Smithsonian Marine Ecosystems Exhibit at the St. Lucie County Aquarium in Fort Pierce welcomes visitors to discover Florida's coastal habitats through immersive encounters with marine life. Located at 420 Seaway Drive, the facility operates year-round and has maintained a distinctive approach to ocean education since 1980. Manager Bill Hoffman describes the aquarium's commitment to displaying fully functional, complex ecosystem models. "We feel like we're the best kept secret on the Treasure Coast, and we don't want to be," Hoffman said. The facility houses more species than many larger aquariums, offering visitors a unique educational experience.

The centerpiece of the exhibit is the Atlantic coral reef tank, a large display that recreates one of Florida's most important coastal ecosystems. Beyond the coral reef, visitors encounter live exhibits representing seagrass beds, mangroves, and hardbottom communities. These displays demonstrate how different marine organisms interact and depend on one another. The exhibits even include smaller creatures, such as a four-inch barracuda, highlighting the diversity found within these ecosystems. According to Hoffman, understanding the importance of small organisms is essential to appreciating how stable ecosystems function.

A popular attraction within the exhibit is the touch tank, where guests can handle unusual marine species under the supervision of trained staff. Exhibit educator Chelsie Corcoran notes that visitors often encounter animals they have never encountered before in this hands-on environment. This interactive component allows guests of all ages to engage directly with marine life and develop a deeper connection to ocean conservation.

The Smithsonian Marine Ecosystems Exhibit operates in partnership with the Smithsonian Marine Station to educate the public about ocean threats while promoting conservation efforts. As concerns about ocean health grow, exhibits like this one serve an important role in connecting visitors to the fragile ecosystems of Florida's coastal waters. The facility is celebrating its 25th anniversary later this year with special programming. For more information about the aquarium and its exhibits, visitors can check sms.si.edu and the Smithsonian Marine Station's social media channels.

cards.headline: Hundreds of fish die in Port St. Lucie Sawgrass Lakes community after city algae treatment
cards.teaser: Residents found hundreds of dead fish floating in their backyards Thursday morning after the city hired SOLitude to treat water for algae on Tuesday and Wednesday.
cards.body:
Dead fish floated across the Sawgrass Lakes community in Port St. Lucie on Thursday morning following an algae treatment conducted earlier in the week. The city hired vendor SOLitude to treat the water for algae on Tuesday and Wednesday. Neighbor Jim Herbert reported seeing "hundreds and hundreds of fish here, and thousands of those little ones just gulping the air." Experts explained that the combination of high heat and algae treatment can render water uninhabitable for aquatic life. On Thursday, city crews removed dead fish from the area and tested oxygen levels in the water.

City official Scott Samples said the city has been working with neighbors and other cities and counties to find solutions, though he noted options depend on factors not yet resolved. Jim Moir, executive director of the Indian Riverkeeper, recommended the city pursue natural solutions including planting aquatic vegetation, reducing fertilizer use, and removing sediment that fuels algae growth. Moir warned the city will end up in a cycle it cannot break unless it returns to natural remediation. Herbert noted this marked at least the second fish die-off since he has lived in the community.

cards.headline: Wellington posts highest rents in Palm Beach County while Belle Glade offers cheapest housing
cards.teaser: Fair Market Rent in Wellington ZIP code 33449 reaches nearly $2,850 for a one-bedroom apartment and exceeds $5,080 monthly for four-bedroom homes, according to new 2026 HUD data.
cards.body:
Wellington residents face the highest rental costs in Palm Beach County, with Fair Market Rent reaching nearly $2,850 for a one-bedroom apartment, according to 2026 data from the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development. ZIP code 33449 in Wellington posted the county's highest Fair Market Rent rates, with four-bedroom homes exceeding $5,080 monthly. Belle Glade offers the county's most affordable rental market at $890 for comparable housing. HUD's Fair Market Rent data shows substantial price variations across South Florida counties, with one-bedroom apartments ranging from $890 in Belle Glade to $1,032 in Okeechobee County, $1,222 in Indian River County, and $1,467 in the St. Lucie and Martin areas.

Real estate broker Talbot Sutter, president of Sutter and Nugent Real Estate, attributes Wellington's high costs to quality amenities and top A-rated school districts, along with lifestyle factors including equestrian and outdoor activities. Sutter works with high-end clients, often executives from New York City, who rent luxury properties before purchasing. He identifies the priciest rental markets in Wellington, western Lake Worth, Delray Beach and Boca Raton. Luis Rivera, who lives in Section 8 housing in Palm Beach County, said budgeting is necessary as rents exceed two or three thousand dollars even in unreasonable neighborhoods. Joanne Bromfield recently relocated from Tampa after a 12-year education career and switched to real estate, finding Palm Beach County rental prices expensive.

cards.headline: Fresh produce prices climb more than 6% as Palm Beach County shoppers switch to frozen alternatives
cards.teaser: One in three American families now purchase fewer fresh fruits and vegetables due to rising costs, while 20% have switched to frozen alternatives, according to a new study from Advance America.
cards.body:
Palm Beach County shoppers are changing their grocery buying habits as fresh fruit and vegetable prices climbed more than 6% over the past year, according to Thursday's federal inflation report and new consumer research from financial services company Advance America. One in three American families now purchase fewer fresh fruits and vegetables due to rising costs, while 20% have switched to frozen alternatives. Some shoppers told WPTV they are adapting their purchasing strategies, with one Palm Beach County resident explaining that frozen organic produce offers the same quality at comparable prices to fresh options. Another shopper described visiting Don Victor's in Lake Worth for vegetables, noting his shopping day now consists of two or three stops to find better deals on fresh produce.

Federal data shows overall grocery prices increased 2.7% year-over-year through May, with fresh produce leading the increases at more than 6%. The Advance America study found Florida residents now spend over $28 more monthly on groceries compared to previous periods. The shift toward frozen and canned alternatives could have lasting effects on local grocery retailers and consumer nutrition habits, even as some shoppers find creative ways to maintain access to fresh produce through strategic shopping at multiple stores.

cards.headline: Indian River County faces $50 million budget loss from property tax amendment on November ballot
cards.teaser: Indian River County could lose around $50 million from its $597 million budget if voters approve a property tax amendment on the November ballot, according to p.
cards.body:
Indian River County leaders gathered Friday morning at the Heritage Center in Vero Beach to discuss the potential financial impact of a property tax amendment on this November's ballot. The amendment would raise the homestead exemption to $150,000 in 2027 and $250,000 in 2028. According to the Indian River County Tax Payers Association, the county's approximately $597 million budget could lose around $50 million by 2028. Vice Chair Laura Moss criticized the measure as unsound public policy, saying "They've declared war on local government." Lance Lunceford, president of the Tax Payers Association, stated there is no way to fill a hole that size without reducing law enforcement and first responder services.

Indian River Firefighters president Christen Brewer warned that fire rescue could lose $15 to $20 million of its $70 million budget, noting that 79.1% of fire rescue funding comes from ad valorem taxes. Three projected fire stations may not be built if the budget shortfall occurs. Lunceford characterized the amendment as a tax shift rather than a tax cut, potentially requiring the county to increase impact fees, utility fees, and taxes on non-homesteaded and commercial properties to compensate for lost revenue.

cards.headline: Governor DeSantis announces Medicaid fraud crackdown in West Palm Beach targeting fake providers
cards.teaser: More than a dozen entities presenting themselves as Medicaid providers in West Palm Beach were actually staged operations created solely to steal from the state program, officials revealed.
cards.body:
Governor Ron DeSantis announced sweeping Medicaid fraud prevention measures Friday afternoon in West Palm Beach, targeting sophisticated criminal operations that have cost Florida taxpayers millions of dollars. Speaking at the Health Care District of Palm Beach County, DeSantis said the state is partnering with President Donald Trump's administration and federal agencies to combat Medicaid fraud, which he identified as particularly concentrated in southeast Florida, including Miami-Dade and Broward counties.

Agency for Healthcare Administration Secretary Shevaun L. Harris revealed that more than a dozen entities presenting themselves as Medicaid providers in West Palm Beach were staged operations created solely to steal from the state program. Investigators discovered the fake operations through shared addresses across multiple unrelated entities, suspicious ownership structures, and no evidence of actual patient care. The state announced three major initiatives: a pilot program with identity fraud detection company Ventolin, enrollment moratoriums on high-risk provider categories including durable medical equipment suppliers and adult day care providers, and comprehensive revalidation requiring all active Florida Medicaid providers to verify credentials and identity. Harris said Florida's program integrity efforts have already saved $136.45 million in recovery and prevention benefits, and over the past two years AHCA has terminated or denied enrollment to more than 3,200 providers. Florida's Medicaid program covers nearly 4 million recipients statewide.

cards.headline: Daughter of St. Lucie County Florida Turnpike crash victim files wrongful death lawsuit
cards.teaser: Angeline Dowdian, 22, filed a wrongful death lawsuit against truck driver Harjinder Singh, White Hawk Carriers, and freight broker C.H. Robinson after the August 12, 2025 crash that killed her mother Faniola Joseph and two others.
cards.body:
Angeline Dowdian, 22, has filed a wrongful death lawsuit against truck driver Harjinder Singh, White Hawk Carriers, and freight broker C.H. Robinson following an August 12, 2025 crash in St. Lucie County that killed her mother Faniola Joseph, 37, along with Herby Dufresne, 30, and Rodrigue Dor, 54. The three were traveling in a minivan when Singh allegedly attempted an illegal U-turn in a clearly marked "No U-turn" zone on the Florida Turnpike, causing the minivan to become wedged underneath his semi-truck. The lawsuit alleges negligence and unsafe practices. Attorney Dax Bello of Stuart Tillman, Fox, Bianchi & Kane argues the crash was not an accident but "a predictable end that came at the cost of three lives."

The lawsuit alleges that C.H. Robinson, a multibillion-dollar freight broker, knowingly gave business to White Hawk Carriers despite serious safety violations in its record. Transportation expert James Lewis has described White Hawk's violations as "very egregious." The case is strengthened by a May 14 U.S. Supreme Court ruling in Montgomery v. Caribbean Transport, which clarified that federal law does not shield freight brokers from state negligence claims when unsafe drivers are placed on the road. Singh faces criminal traffic homicide charges in Florida in addition to the civil case. White Hawk Carriers has since shut down.

hero.headline: Smithsonian Marine Exhibit at Fort Pierce aquarium showcases Florida coastal ecosystems with live coral reef tank
hero.body:
The Smithsonian Marine Ecosystems Exhibit at the St. Lucie County Aquarium invites visitors to experience Florida's underwater habitats through live displays of the state's most important coastal environments. Located at 420 Seaway Drive in Fort Pierce, the facility offers close encounters with marine life in the waterfront district. Manager Bill Hoffman explains that the aquarium's approach of displaying fully living, complex ecosystem models has been central to its mission since 1980, setting it apart from most other public aquariums. "We feel like we're the best kept secret on the Treasure Coast, and we don't want to be," Hoffman told WPTV, noting that the facility houses more species than many larger exhibits.

The Atlantic coral reef tank serves as the exhibit's centerpiece, recreating one of Florida's most significant coastal ecosystems in vivid detail. Beyond the reef display, visitors encounter live models of seagrass beds, mangroves, and hardbottom communities. Each exhibit demonstrates how different organisms interact within their environment. The aquarium even features a four-inch barracuda, offering visitors an unexpected look at a predator in miniature form. These diverse displays help illustrate the complexity of Florida's marine world to guests of all ages.

The touch tank remains a popular attraction where visitors can handle unusual marine species under staff supervision. According to exhibit educator Chelsie Corcoran, guests often encounter animals they have never touched before. The hands-on experience deepens visitor connection to marine life. The facility plans upcoming programming tied to its 25th anniversary celebration later this year, continuing its commitment to visitor engagement and education.

Operating in partnership with the Smithsonian Marine Station, the exhibit works to increase public awareness about ocean health challenges while promoting conservation. Hoffman emphasizes that functioning ecosystems depend on countless small organisms, a concept reinforced through the live displays throughout the facility. With rising concerns about ocean health, exhibits like this one offer valuable educational opportunities for understanding Florida's fragile marine ecosystems. The aquarium is open to the public year-round. Visitors seeking more information can visit sms.si.edu or check the Smithsonian Marine Station's social media channels.

cards.headline: Curaçao's World Cup soccer team draws Port St. Lucie fans to Boca Raton training ahead of historic debut
cards.teaser: Some Curaçao natives made the drive from Port St. Lucie to watch the team's training session at Florida Atlantic University stadium before the island nation's first-ever World Cup match Sunday against Germany.
cards.body:
Hundreds of soccer fans gathered at Florida Atlantic University stadium in Boca Raton on Thursday to watch Curaçao's national team train ahead of its historic first-ever World Cup appearance this weekend. The team, known as the "Blue Wave," drew enthusiastic supporters from across South Florida and beyond. Marionella Barzeycoggins, originally from Curaçao, made the drive from Port St. Lucie with her entire family after learning about the training event and securing an RSVP.

Curaçao, an island nation with a population of just over 150,000 people, is the smallest nation to qualify for the tournament and went undefeated in all 10 of its 2026 World Cup qualifying matches. Goalkeeper Eloy Room told WPTV that the crowd's support has energized the team ahead of competition. Midfielder Tahitch Chong said the moment carries enormous meaning for the players and the entire island. Local fan Bruce Zalman described the energy as incredible and expressed hope to attend games at the Hard Rock. Curaçao faces Germany this Sunday in Houston, Texas.

cards.headline: Palm Beach County deputy pulls over Lake Worth woman for holding phone in hand she was born without
cards.teaser: Katie Thomas was cited for allegedly holding her phone in her right hand while driving, but the Lake Worth woman was born without a right hand. The case was dropped for lack of evidence after body camera footage went viral with 110 million views.
cards.body:
A Palm Beach County deputy pulled over Katie Thomas of Lake Worth for allegedly holding her phone in her right hand while driving. The traffic stop went viral on social media, generating 110 million views. Body camera footage shows the deputy telling Thomas what he observed, saying "You drove past me, holding the phone with your right hand, manipulating that phone." Thomas responded by raising her arm to show her stump. She was born without her right hand and has spent her life as an adaptive athlete, raising awareness for the limb-difference community. "Literally being accused of something that I did not have a limb to be accused. I think that's what's probably one of the most captivating things about the whole thing, is that it was immediate, immediately apparent to 110 million people, that what he claims he saw was impossible," Thomas said.

The citation was dropped for lack of evidence. The Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office said an agency review of the case is underway. Thomas said she harbors no ill will against the sheriff's office and would be open to a conversation about using the moment to spread awareness about the limb difference community. She started selling "Hand to God" merchandise on her Instagram, with proceeds benefiting Shriners Children's Hospital. Thomas said she has no plans to sue and hopes the attention helps people better understand the limb difference community.

cards.headline: Humane Society of the Treasure Coast thrift stores house cats during Palm City shelter renovation
cards.teaser: The Humane Society of the Treasure Coast is using its two thrift stores in Stuart to keep animal care going during a major renovation of its shelter in Palm City.
cards.body:
The Humane Society of the Treasure Coast is temporarily housing adoptable cats at its two thrift stores while undergoing major renovations at its Palm City shelter. The nonprofit began construction on its adoption, customer service, and intake areas earlier this year, shifting many cats to the store locations, according to spokesperson Sarah Fisher. "With our shelter cages unavailable, the stores have become a lifeline for our animals," Fisher explained Thursday. Senior Manager Kelly Ellis said shoppers can now find both unique items for sale and adoptable cats at both locations.

The thrift stores are located at 3302 SE Federal Highway in Stuart and 1099 NW 21st St, Stuart. Ellis noted that "every treasure you find here helps provide for our animals" and added that donations of gently used goods are welcome. The organization is currently seeking temporary foster homes for other animals while construction continues. Store hours and donation guidelines are available at hstc1.org.

cards.headline: Delray Beach Public Library offers free STREAM summer programs for kids and teens
cards.teaser: The Delray Beach Public Library is making summer brighter for kids and teens with free STREAM programs in Science, Technology, Reading, Art, Engineering and Math, open to all Florida residents.
cards.body:
The Delray Beach Public Library is offering free STREAM summer programs for kids and teens, open to all Florida residents. Kae Jonsons, director of development and community relations, told WPTV the library has served the community since 1913, when 30 women from the Ladies Improvement Society each donated a book to start the collection. Today, the library welcomes more than 193,000 visitors annually to its 36,000 square foot facility at Atlantic Avenue and Swinton Avenue.

Young adult librarian Natalie Baron is leading sessions like ColorSpace: Artistic Excavations, where teens explore art history from cave paintings to ancient pottery. Teens can also join lab-based activities including collaborative 3D puzzle builds and pick up themed book boxes. Mandy Fulop, head of the children's department, is launching the STREAM Into Summer Literacy Program, encouraging young readers to set goals with librarians, track progress, and take home an Unearth a Story bag with a free STREAM book and activities. In partnership with the School District of Palm Beach County, the library serves free lunch daily from 11:30 a.m. to 12:30 p.m. and snacks from 2 p.m. to 4 p.m. to youth up to 18. Family Nights on select Tuesdays invite children 5 and older to explore STREAM topics together. Saturday Science Discovery programs for ages 9 to 12 feature hands-on archaeology activities. Registration is available at delraylibrary.org.

hero.headline: Florida economy to add 2.3 million residents by 2035 despite downgraded tourism and income forecasts
hero.body:
Florida will gain approximately 2.3 million residents between 2026 and 2035 while continuing to outpace national economic growth, according to a new economic outlook from Florida TaxWatch. The state's population is expected to grow from 23.8 million in 2026 to just over 26 million by 2035. Despite these gains, daily net migration will gradually decline from about 895 people per day to 689. Florida's appeal remains strong thanks to its business climate, absence of a personal income tax, and favorable weather, allowing the state to attract new residents even as economic headwinds persist.

The latest TaxWatch report reflects significant downgrades compared to previous forecasts. The organization cited global instability, rising energy costs, and uncertainty regarding the Strait of Hormuz as primary concerns. The statewide unemployment rate is projected to peak at 4.8% in 2027 before gradually settling near 4.2% in the early 2030s. Per-capita personal income is still expected to increase from roughly $88,000 in 2026 to more than $126,000 by 2035, but overall income projections have declined by an average of 10.3% from the prior forecast. Total employment will grow from 10.1 million workers to 11.3 million over the decade.

Tourism experienced the steepest downgrade of any sector, with visitor growth expectations falling by an average of 45.3% since the previous report. Visitor numbers are still projected to increase annually, but growth rates will slow dramatically, reaching just 0.8% growth next year. This represents the most significant impact from current economic uncertainties on Florida's major industries.

Florida's broader economy is expected to weather these challenges without major disruption. Real GDP growth will decelerate from 2.5% in 2026 to 1.9% in 2027, then rebound above 3% for much of the following decade, which actually represents an improvement compared to TaxWatch's previous forecast. According to the report, the single biggest variable shaping the outlook is uncertainty surrounding the Strait of Hormuz, through which approximately a quarter of the world's seaborne oil passes. Should energy markets stabilize, many of the more pessimistic assumptions in the forecast could improve. If not, Florida residents may face a more challenging economic path ahead.

cards.headline: José Javier Rodríguez wins Democratic nomination for Florida Attorney General by default
cards.teaser: Former state Senator José Javier Rodríguez earned the Democratic nomination for Florida Attorney General Friday after no other Democrats challenged him, setting up a November matchup with appointed incumbent James Uthmeier.
cards.body:
Former state Senator José Javier Rodríguez secured the Democratic nomination for Florida Attorney General on Friday by default, as no other Democrats challenged incumbent Attorney General James Uthmeier. Rodríguez, a former Assistant Labor Secretary, said he is honored to be the nominee and committed to focusing his campaign on three issues: tackling crime, reducing higher costs, and addressing corruption in Tallahassee. Uthmeier was appointed last year by Ron DeSantis after serving the Governor as Chief of Staff among other roles.

Rodríguez plans to travel the state between now and November to present his case directly to voters as the People's Lawyer, promising to make communities safer, bring down costs for working families, and hold the powerful accountable. However, he faces a significant cash disadvantage heading into the general election. Rodríguez has raised roughly $641,000 and spent approximately $366,000 thus far, while Uthmeier has raised more than $1.3 million and spent roughly $266,000. An associated political committee, Friends of James Uthmeier, has raised more than $7.8 million and spent less than $770,000.

cards.headline: Former House Speaker Paul Renner accuses Florida GOP of blocking gubernatorial debates to favor Byron Donalds
cards.teaser: Paul Renner criticized the Republican Party of Florida for refusing to stage a debate at the Sunshine Showdown event, arguing the party is tipping the scales in favor of Donald Trump-endorsed frontrunner Byron Donalds.
cards.body:
Former House Speaker Paul Renner accused the Republican Party of Florida of rigging the gubernatorial primary in favor of U.S. Rep. Byron Donalds by refusing to stage a debate at the upcoming Sunshine Showdown event. The party asserted that only Donalds met the qualification criteria: 10% support in the RPOF's own poll, more than $10 million raised, and more than 10,000 donors. Renner questioned whether the party still believes in free competition, asking voters be allowed to decide who has the experience, delivered results, and has the vision to lead. He echoed Gov. Ron DeSantis' criticism that Donalds was not part of his administration's battles against the left.

Renner also blasted the party for discouraging independent debates that were routine in statewide primary races until this cycle, questioning what happened to the First Amendment. At least two media-run debates have been proposed but discouraged by the party. At a Friday press conference, DeSantis said the party has a limited role and the process should be candidate-driven. At the later event, Renner, Donalds, and Lt. Jay Collins will speak to voters separately without sharing a stage. Fourth candidate James Fishback was denied the opportunity to speak after committing to an unsanctioned television debate and for what Chairman Evan Power described as antisemitic and racist attacks on party members.

cards.headline: Governor DeSantis orders flags lowered at Florida Capitol and in Brevard County for former Congressman Bill Posey
cards.teaser: Ron DeSantis directed flags at the Capitol, Brevard County Courthouse, and Palm Bay City Hall to fly at half staff Saturday in honor of former U.S. Representative Bill Posey, who died at age 78 last month.
cards.body:
Governor Ron DeSantis has directed flags at the Capitol, Brevard County Courthouse, and Palm Bay City Hall to fly at half staff on Saturday in honor of former U.S. Representative Bill Posey, who died at age 78 last month. A Republican, Posey served in Congress for 16 years. Before his election to Congress, he served in both chambers of the Florida Legislature, eight years in each. "Former Representative Posey lived an honorable life of service and always displayed his unwavering dedication to the citizens of Florida. Our prayers go out to his family," DeSantis wrote Friday in his directive.

Following Posey's death, U.S. Representative Mike Haridopolos, a Republican, posted a tribute to the former representative. "Throughout his career, he earned a reputation as a principled conservative, a steadfast advocate for fiscal responsibility and government transparency, and a tireless supporter of America's space program and the communities he proudly represented along Florida's Space Coast," Haridopolos wrote. Posey was cofounder of the Congressional Estuary Caucus.

cards.headline: Florida Supreme Court declines to halt new congressional map implementation for midterm elections
cards.teaser: The Florida Supreme Court denied a petition from voting rights groups urging justices to put the state's new congressional map on hold for the midterm elections, allowing the redistricting to proceed.
cards.body:
The Florida Supreme Court has declined to intervene in efforts to block implementation of a new congressional map before the midterm elections. Voting rights groups, including the Equal Ground Protection Fund, had petitioned the court to halt the map's use, arguing that deploying it this year could harm voters if it were later found to be illegal. A Leon County circuit judge previously rejected a request for an injunction on the map, and the 1st District Court of Appeal declined to reverse that decision.

In a 6-1 majority decision, the Supreme Court justices stated they would not step into the process. "At this time, we do not have jurisdiction over that matter, and we do not simply assume that the 1st District's decision will provide an appropriate basis for this Court's review," the justices wrote. The ruling removes the final legal obstacle to implementing the new congressional map for the upcoming midterm elections.

cards.headline: Florida statewide races finalized after qualifying week ends with fields set for November
cards.teaser: Qualifying week ended with the Republican gubernatorial field including U.S. Representative Jay Collins, former House Speaker Paul Renner, and James Fishback alongside several unknowns, while Democrat David Jolly and running mate Gwen Graham are also confirmed.
cards.body:
Qualifying week concluded with several matchups confirmed for Florida's statewide races. The Attorney General race will feature Democratic former Senator José Javier Rodríguez against appointed incumbent Republican James Uthmeier. For Chief Financial Officer, appointed incumbent Blaise Ingoglia will face the winner of a Democratic Primary between former Senator Annette Taddeo and Earle Ford. Agriculture Commissioner Wilton Simpson will compete against the winner of a Democratic Primary between two relative unknowns.

The Republican Party of Florida set stringent criteria for gubernatorial debate participation, requiring candidates to reach 10 percent support in the party's own poll, raise more than $10 million, and secure more than 10,000 donors. Under these rules, only one candidate qualified, prompting the party to allow candidates to speak individually rather than debate. Republican candidates have urged their competitor into debate, but the campaign responded that it is not in the business of handing out participation trophies.

cards.headline: Lee Steinhauer exits Florida House District 45 race, endorses Erin Huntley in bid for Republican unity
cards.teaser: Winter Garden lawyer Lee Steinhauer ended his campaign Friday for Florida House District 45 and threw his support behind Orange County GOP Chair Erin Huntley, clearing her path to face Democratic Representative Leonard Spencer in November.
cards.body:
Lee Steinhauer, a Winter Garden lawyer and president of The Steinhauer Group, ended his campaign Friday and endorsed Erin Huntley in the race for Florida House District 45. Steinhauer announced his withdrawal on Facebook as the qualifying window closed, citing his commitment to his two young sons. "I have two young sons that I want to be there for as they grow up, and while running for political office can wait, their childhoods will not," he wrote. He framed his exit as necessary for Republican unity in a competitive general election, stating: "This will be a tough election cycle and having unity among Republicans will be critical to winning the seat back."

Huntley, the Orange County GOP Chair, has led the Republican primary field since filing in January 2025. She raised more than $252,000 by the end of last year and secured endorsements from U.S. Rep. Daniel Webster, former state Sen. Mike Haridopolos, Agriculture Commissioner Wilton Simpson, Attorney General James Uthmeier, and Osceola Sheriff Christopher Blackmon. Gov. Ron DeSantis appointed her to the Florida Virtual School Board of Trustees earlier in the cycle. Steinhauer filed in April 2025 and loaned his campaign $20,000 but never closed the financial gap. The withdrawal sets up a November matchup between Huntley and Democratic Rep. Leonard Spencer in HD 45, which spans Orange and Osceola counties.

hero.headline: Stuart attorney represents daughter of Florida Turnpike crash victim in wrongful death lawsuit
hero.body:
Angeline Dowdian, 22, has filed a wrongful death lawsuit against truck driver Harjinder Singh, White Hawk Carriers, and freight broker C.H. Robinson following the August 12, 2025 crash in St. Lucie County that killed her mother Faniola Joseph, 37, and two others. The crash occurred when Singh allegedly attempted an illegal U-turn in a clearly marked No U-turn zone on the Florida Turnpike, causing the minivan carrying Joseph, Herby Dufresne, 30, and Rodrigue Dor, 54, to become wedged underneath his semi-truck. All three people in the minivan were killed.

Angeline is represented by attorney Dax Bello of Stuart firm Tillman, Fox, Bianchi & Kane, and co-counsel Mark Brumer of Brumer & Brumer. The lawsuit alleges that C.H. Robinson, a multibillion-dollar freight broker, knowingly gave business to White Hawk Carriers despite serious safety violations in its record. Transportation expert James Lewis has publicly described White Hawk's violations as very egregious. Bello argues the crash was not an accident but a predictable end that came at the cost of three lives.

The case is bolstered by a May 14 U.S. Supreme Court ruling in Montgomery v. Caribbean Transport, which clarified that federal law does not shield freight brokers from state negligence claims when unsafe drivers are placed on the road. That ruling involved the same broker named in Angeline's case. Justice Brett Kavanaugh wrote in a concurring opinion that not all truck accidents can be prevented, but some can, noting that some carriers are known to be less safe and some truck drivers are known to be unfit.

Angeline lived in another country at the time of the crash and had not seen her mother in person in six years, though they spoke daily via video calls. On the day of the crash, she missed a call from her mother. She listens to a voice message from her mother every morning that says, Angeline, where are you? Angeline says her mother was both parents to her, since her father rejected her at birth. Singh faces criminal traffic homicide charges in Florida in addition to the civil case. White Hawk Carriers has shut down, though Bello warns they may reopen under another name.

hero.headline: Fort Pierce shooting leaves 16-year-old in critical condition, teen charged with attempted homicide
hero.teaser: A 16-year-old is facing an attempted homicide charge after a shooting Thursday night in Fort Pierce left another 16-year-old in critical condition.
hero.body:
A 16-year-old is facing an attempted homicide charge after a shooting Thursday night in Fort Pierce. According to Fort Pierce police, detectives from the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office heard gunshots while traveling on Avenue N and saw three juveniles fleeing in different directions. Another juvenile was discovered laying on the sidewalk on top of a bike with gunshot wounds.

Detectives and officers established a perimeter in the area and apprehended all three suspects. One suspect was caught by a sheriff's office K9, and another was found hiding in a recycling container. Two weapons were recovered at the scene. The 16-year-old victim remained in critical condition at a local hospital as of Friday morning. The 16-year-old suspect was arrested and charged with attempted homicide, tampering with evidence and unlawful carry of a firearm by a person under 18. He was taken to the Department of Juvenile Justice.

Joseph had been living in Indiana and came south to purchase goods to resell in her shop. The lawsuit alleges that C.H. Robinson, a multibillion-dollar freight broker, knowingly gave business to White Hawk Carriers despite serious safety violations in its record. Transportation expert James Lewis has publicly described White Hawk's violations as "very egregious." The case is strengthened by a May 14 U.S. Supreme Court ruling in Montgomery v. Caribbean Transport, which clarified that federal law does not shield freight brokers from state negligence claims when unsafe drivers are placed on the road. The highlight is the Atlantic coral reef exhibit, a sprawling tank that recreates one of Florida's most significant coastal ecosystems. Visitors will also see live models of seagrass beds, mangroves, and hardbottom communities, each demonstrating the intricate relationships between organisms. The exhibit's touch tank allows guests to handle unusual marine species under staff guidance, according to exhibit educator Chelsie Corcoran.

The Smithsonian Marine Ecosystems Exhibit operates in partnership with the Smithsonian Marine Station, aiming to raise public awareness about threats facing oceans while inspiring conservation. Upcoming programming will tie into the facility's 25th anniversary celebration later this year. The facility is located at 420 Seaway Drive in Fort Pierce and is open to the public year-round. More information can be found at sms.si.edu and on their Smithsonian Marine Station social media channels.

hero.headline: Port St. Lucie teen makes history as Southeast Youth of the Year, heads to national competition
hero.teaser: Enrique Rosario Liz, valedictorian of Port St. Lucie High School, became the first member of Boys & Girls Clubs of St. Lucie County to be named Southeast Region Youth of the Year.
hero.body:
Enrique Rosario Liz has achieved a historic milestone as the first-ever member of Boys & Girls Clubs of St. Lucie County to be named Southeast Region Youth of the Year. The Port St. Lucie High School valedictorian will now travel to New York City on October 1 to compete for the national Youth of the Year title. This prestigious award recognizes exceptional teens across the Boys & Girls Clubs community who demonstrate academic excellence, strong values, and commitment to serving others.

Enrique's path to this achievement reflects remarkable personal growth. He arrived in Florida from the Dominican Republic eight years ago without speaking English. Rather than letting this barrier hold him back, he embraced support from his school and the local Boys & Girls Club to develop his skills and confidence. "I could never have imagined this moment when I was 8 years old," Enrique said after receiving the award. "It's a privilege to share my journey, and I hope it inspires belief in every young person who needs a helping hand and an opportunity." His determination transformed him from a newcomer into an academic leader, culminating in his graduation as valedictorian this spring. He will attend the University of Florida in the fall.

Leaders throughout the community have recognized Enrique's character and potential. Will Armstead, CEO of Boys & Girls Clubs of St. Lucie County, highlighted what sets Enrique apart. "Enrique's achievement is historic, but his character impresses me most. He's turned challenges into opportunities and advocated for others, all with humility and determination," Armstead said. Travis Leonard, owner of A&G Concrete Pools and a longtime Youth of the Year judge, also voiced his confidence in Enrique's readiness for national competition. "From the start, Enrique stood out. Thanks to his hard work and all those who support him, we finally have a Southeast Region Youth of the Year. I believe he's ready for the national competition, and I'm proud of him and our whole community," Leonard said.

Enrique's family has expressed their gratitude for the opportunities that helped shape his success. His parents emphasized their appreciation for both divine blessing and institutional support. "We're grateful to God for every opportunity and to Boys & Girls Clubs of St. Lucie County for helping Enrique grow as a leader and a person," they said. As Enrique prepares to represent the Southeast region on the national stage, his journey continues to inspire young people throughout the community and demonstrates the transformative power of opportunity and determination.

cards.headline: Vero Beach man charged with murdering 76-year-old grandmother who welcomed him into her home
cards.teaser: Nicholas Leonard Ivey, 29, faces murder and evidence tampering charges in the death of his grandmother, who was found dead in her Vero Beach home in February.
cards.body:
The Indian River County Sheriff's Office announced Friday that 29-year-old Nicholas Leonard Ivey now faces charges of murder and tampering with physical evidence in the death of 76-year-old Patricia Ann DiBella. Investigators said Ivey admitted to killing DiBella, his grandmother, who had opened her home to him at her residence at 5090 Fairways Circle north of Vero Beach. On February 1, a welfare check was requested by family members, which led deputies to the scene where Ivey was taken into custody. The sheriff's office said he was formally charged with murder on June 3. Since February, Ivey has been held on other related charges and is currently being held at the Indian River County Jail without bond.

Sheriff Eric Flowers said in a statement, "I am proud of the work our investigations team did to bring justice to Patricia DiBella and her family. No one should lose their life at the hands of someone they trusted and welcomed into their home. I encourage anyone experiencing domestic violence to contact law enforcement." The Indian River County Sheriff's Office reminded the community that domestic violence can take many forms and can affect anyone. Anyone in danger is urged to call 911, SafeSpace at 772-288-7023, or the National Domestic Violence Hotline at 1-800-799-7233.

cards.headline: Indian River County warns property tax amendment could cut $50 million from budget
cards.teaser: Indian River County could lose around $50 million in funding by 2028 if voters approve a property tax amendment on the November ballot, county leaders warned Fr.
cards.body:
Indian River County leaders gathered Friday at the Heritage Center in Vero Beach to warn residents about a property tax amendment on the November ballot. The amendment would raise the homestead exemption to $150,000 in 2027 and $250,000 in 2028, potentially costing the county around $50 million in funding by 2028. Laura Moss, vice chair of the Indian River County Commission, and Lance Lunceford, president of the Indian River County Tax Payers Association, discussed the revenue loss with neighbors and community leaders. According to the Tax Payers Association, the county operates on a budget of approximately $597 million, making the projected loss substantial for the region.

Lunceford characterized the amendment as a tax shift rather than a tax cut, warning that the county could raise taxes on non-homesteaded and commercial properties to compensate for lost revenue through increased impact fees and utility fees. Christen Brewer, president of Indian River Firefighters, stated that fire rescue could lose $15 to $20 million of their $70 million budget, with 79.1 percent of their funding coming from ad valorem taxes. Brewer noted that three projected fire stations may not be built if the budget shortfall occurs. Moss criticized the state's role in the amendment, calling it "an unsound, unplanned piece of public policy."

cards.headline: 28-year-old West Palm Beach motorcyclist killed in Boynton Beach crash
cards.teaser: Albert Garcia died Friday morning after his motorcycle struck a car at the intersection of Boynton Beach Boulevard and El Clair Ranch Road.
cards.body:
A 28-year-old West Palm Beach man was killed Friday morning in a crash involving a motorcycle and a car at the intersection of Boynton Beach Boulevard and El Clair Ranch Road. The crash happened around 7:08 a.m., according to the Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office.

Investigators said Albert Garcia was riding a 2007 Kawasaki Ninja eastbound on Boynton Beach Boulevard at a high rate of speed as he approached the intersection. At the same time, a 2016 Kia Forte driven by a 39-year-old Boynton Beach man was stopped in the westbound lanes of Boynton Beach Boulevard and attempting to make a left turn onto southbound El Clair Ranch Road. As the Kia began turning left, Garcia applied the motorcycle's brakes but did not have enough time or distance to avoid a collision. The motorcycle struck the passenger side of the Kia inside the intersection, and Garcia was thrown from the motorcycle, landing a short distance southwest of the impact point. Rescue crews transported Garcia to Delray Medical Center, where he was pronounced dead. The driver of the Kia was wearing a seatbelt and was not injured. Garcia was wearing a helmet at the time of the crash.

cards.headline: Delray Beach Pride memorial effort faces new state restrictions on 10th anniversary of Pulse massacre
cards.teaser: The Delray Beach Pride Memorial Committee has designed a rainbow pyramid monument to honor the 49 victims of the Pulse nightclub massacre, but a new state bill threatens to block the project.
cards.body:
Friday, June 12 marks 10 years since the Pulse nightclub massacre in Orlando, where 49 people lost their lives. In Delray Beach, a rainbow-painted Pride intersection created to honor the victims was sandblasted away in August 2025 by the Florida Department of Transportation to comply with a statewide push to regulate road markings and remove political and ideological messaging. Local advocate Ronnie Dunayer said community members had paid for the mural themselves out of sadness over the tragedy.

The Delray Beach Pride Memorial Committee, formed by Dunayer and other residents, designed a proposal by March for a rainbow pyramid monument etched with the meaning behind each color, to be illuminated at night and placed at Old School Square near the Eagle Scout monument. Commissioner Juli Casal cited Senate Bill 1134 as a legal obstacle. The bill, awaiting the governor's decision and having passed 25-11 in the Senate and 77-37 in the House, would ban local governments from funding or supporting diversity, equity and inclusion initiatives. Casal stated the two major hurdles are using city money for the memorial and placing it on city land. She said if private funding and private property were found, the project could be completed immediately. Dunayer is reaching out to state leaders and national organizations to find solutions.

cards.headline: Daughter of Florida Turnpike crash victim files wrongful death lawsuit, speaks out for first time
cards.teaser: Angeline Dowdian filed a wrongful death lawsuit against a truck driver and two companies after her mother, Faniola Joseph, was killed in a St. Lucie County crash in August 2025.
cards.body:
On August 12, 2025, Herby Dufresne, 30, Faniola Joseph, 37, and Rodrigue Dor, 54, were traveling for work in St. Lucie County when their minivan became wedged underneath a semi-truck driven by Harjinder Singh. Singh allegedly attempted an illegal U-turn in a clearly marked "No U-turn" zone. All three people in the minivan were killed. Joseph's 22-year-old daughter, Angeline Dowdian, has filed a wrongful death lawsuit against Singh, White Hawk Carriers, and freight broker C.H. Robinson, alleging negligence and unsafe practices.

Angeline lived in another country at the time of the crash and had not seen her mother in person in six years, though they spoke daily via video calls. She is represented by attorney Dax Bello of Stuart Tillman, Fox, Bianchi & Kane and co-counsel Mark Brumer. The lawsuit alleges that C.H. Robinson knowingly gave business to White Hawk Carriers despite serious safety violations in its record. Bello says the case is bolstered by a May 14 U.S. Supreme Court ruling in Montgomery v. Caribbean Transport, which clarified that federal law does not shield freight brokers from state negligence claims. Singh faces criminal traffic homicide charges in Florida. White Hawk Carriers has since shut down.

cards.headline: Orlando Health provides health screenings to Indian River County employees
cards.teaser: Orlando Health conducted health screenings for Indian River County government employees.
cards.body: Orlando Health provided health screenings to Indian River County employees, according to Hometown News Treasure Coast. The screenings were conducted for county government workers in Indian River County.
